## Summary: Big Data and the ML Project Pipeline (CFA Level II — Quantitative Methods)

---

### Big Data in Investment Management

**Big data** (alternative data) is data generated by financial markets, businesses, governments, individuals, sensors, and the Internet of Things (IoT). It is distinguished from traditional data by the **3Vs**, plus a fourth "V" that matters especially for inference/prediction:

| Dimension | Definition | Investment Management Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume** | Quantity of data (now measured in petabytes/exabytes, not terabytes) | More signal potentially available, but requires scalable infrastructure |
| **Variety** | Range of sources — structured, semi-structured, unstructured (text, image, video, sensor, clickstream) | Opportunities to augment structured data with alternative data; raises privacy/legal issues |
| **Velocity** | Speed at which data are created (e.g., billions of tweets every few days) | Enables real-time predictive analytics, but "data-in-motion" is harder to analyze than "data-at-rest" |
| **Veracity** | Credibility and reliability of the data source | Social media content can be 10%–15% fake; web spam exceeds 20% of web content; critical to vet sources before use |

> **Key insight**: Veracity is the "fourth V" that matters most for statistical inference and prediction — big data amplifies the classic quality-vs-quantity tradeoff. A large but unreliable dataset can be worse than a smaller, clean one.

**Why it matters for financial forecasting**: Textual big data (news articles, financial forums, social media) offers information faster (real time) and can enhance predictive power versus relying on structured financial/accounting data alone. Textual data provides two key types of information:
- **Topics** — what people are talking about (a firm, industry, event)
- **Sentiment** — how people feel about the topic (positive/negative/neutral)

> One study found positive Twitter sentiment could predict the Dow Jones Industrial Average trend up to three days later with ~87% accuracy.

### Executing a Data Analysis Project: The ML Model Building Steps

Building an ML model using **structured** data follows five sequential (but iterative) steps:

| # | Step | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Conceptualization of the modeling task** | Determine what the model output should be, how it will be used, by whom, and how it fits into business processes |
| 2 | **Data collection** | Gather numeric data, typically already tabular (rows = instances, columns = features) |
| 3 | **Data preparation and wrangling** | Cleanse (fix missing/invalid/inaccurate/inconsistent/non-uniform/duplicate values) and preprocess (extract, aggregate, filter, select) |
| 4 | **Data exploration** | Exploratory data analysis (EDA), feature selection, feature engineering |
| 5 | **Model training** | Select ML method(s), evaluate performance, tune the model |

> **Key insight**: These steps are **iterative** — insights from one iteration can send the project back to reconceptualization. Model building is a loop, not a straight line.

---

### The Text ML Model Building Steps (Unstructured Data)

Textual big data (news articles, social media, internal/external documents) is unstructured. The **first four** steps differ from the structured-data pipeline; the fifth (model training) is essentially the same:

| # | Step (Text) | Corresponding Structured Step | What Changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Text problem formulation** | Conceptualization | Decide exact inputs/outputs (e.g., unstructured text in → structured sentiment score out) and how output will be used |
| 2 | **Data (text) curation** | Data collection | Gather text via web services, spidering/scraping/crawling; may require expert **annotation** with target labels for supervised learning |
| 3 | **Text preparation and wrangling** | Data preparation and wrangling | Cleansing + preprocessing to convert unstructured streams into structured input usable by traditional modeling methods |
| 4 | **Text exploration** | Data exploration | Adds text visualization (e.g., word clouds) alongside text feature selection and engineering |
| 5 | **Model training** | Model training | Same as structured pipeline |

> **Key insight**: The differences in the text pipeline's first four steps reflect the **variety and veracity** dimensions of big data — text requires curation (sourcing/labeling) and wrangling (structuring) steps that numeric data, already tabular, do not need. The resulting **structured output** (e.g., a sentiment score) can then be combined with other structured data or used directly for forecasting.

### Question Set Answers

**Q1 (LendALot Corporation — steps in ML model building for a credit-scoring model using structured data)**:
- **A. Conceptualization**: Decide how model output will be specified (e.g., binary creditworthiness classification), how/by whom it will be used, and how it embeds into business processes.
- **B. Data collection**: Decide whether to use internal, external, or both data sources.
- **C. Data preparation and wrangling**: Decide on cleansing (missing/extreme values) and preprocessing (extracting, aggregating, filtering, selecting) needs.
- **D. Data exploration**: Decide which EDA methods apply, which features to use, and which to engineer.
- **E. Model training**: Choose ML algorithm(s) — supervised, given labeled training data — and decide how fit is measured, validated, and tuned.

**Q2 (Which process step does "enhance the creditworthiness model with text from loan-application free-response fields" address?)**
→ This is the **text problem formulation** step — it defines what unstructured input (free-text responses) will be used to produce what structured output.

**Q3 (Text curation needs for LendALot)**
→ Since the text is **internal** data (loan applications), the team must (1) verify the free-response text fields were correctly implemented/enabled, and (2) ensure a sufficient response rate exists to support analysis (fields may not be mandatory).
